items.title: release-tools
items.text:
The shared release automation of Algorithmiq repositories: release branches, pre-releases (alphas, betas, release candidates), the release PR, release tags, backports, the changelog and the PR checks.

Each repository keeps three short caller stubs, its own publish workflow (because that depends on how the project is built) and a changelog preview recipe. Everything else lives in release-tools, once, and is pinned by tag.

items.title: Where to start
items.text:
• You work in a repository that uses release-tools: The release process, then Releasing and Patch releases. The branching model shows a whole release cycle.
  • You are adopting release-tools in a repository: Adopting release-tools, Per-repository setup, and once per organisation the One-time organisation setup.
  • You maintain release-tools: What is central, Versioning and upgrading, Design, Caveats, Open questions and Developing release-tools.

items.title: Adopting release-tools
items.text: Copy these files, replace v1.2.0 with the current release of release-tools (v1.2.0 or later: the stage input is new in v1.2.0), and use the same tag everywhere. The triggers stay in the stubs: only a repository's own workflow files react to its events. The bot's client ID and private key are passed explicitly rather than through vars inheritance or secrets: inherit: the reusable workflows declare them as a required input and a required secret, so a stub that forgets one fails before anything runs, and no other secret of the repository reaches release-tools.

items.title: .github/workflows/release.yml
items.text:
Set version-files to the files that hold the version number, such as VERSION or pyproject.toml (whose [project] version is updated). Leave it empty if the version comes from the git tag (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs). stage chooses where a release starts (alpha, beta or rc) and promotes a release in beta to release candidates; see Releasing.

# Releases: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
name: Release

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      bump:
        description: "Release to start: next minor or major (patch releases: add the backport label to the fix PR)"
        type: choice
        options: [minor, major]
        default: minor
      stage:
        description: "Stage to start at or promote to (patch releases have no pre-releases)"
        type: choice
        options: [rc, beta, alpha]
        default: rc
  push:
    branches: ["release/**"]
    tags: ["v*"]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  release:
    uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/release.yml@v1.2.0
    with:
      client-id: ${{ vars.RELEASE_BOT_CLIENT_ID }}
      bump: ${{ inputs.bump }}
      stage: ${{ inputs.stage }}
      # Files that hold the version (e.g. "VERSION pyproject.toml"); empty if it
      # comes from the git tag (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs).
      version-files: ""
    secrets:
      private-key: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY }}

items.title: .github/workflows/backport.yml
items.text:
# Backports: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
name: Backport

on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [closed, labeled]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  backport:
    uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/backport.yml@v1.2.0
    with:
      client-id: ${{ vars.RELEASE_BOT_CLIENT_ID }}
    secrets:
      private-key: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY }}

items.title: .github/workflows/pr-checks.yml
items.text:
# PR title and migration notes: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
name: PR checks

on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, edited, reopened, synchronize]

permissions:
  pull-requests: read

jobs:
  # Reports the checks "PR checks / PR title" and "PR checks / Migration notes".
  pr-checks:
    name: PR checks
    uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/pr-checks.yml@v1.2.0

The checks report as PR checks / PR title and PR checks / Migration notes (a called workflow's jobs are named <caller job name> / <job name>). Those are the names to require in the rulesets.

items.title: The publish workflow
items.text:
It must follow this structure: run on push: tags: ["v*"], build and check that the built version matches the tag, create a draft GitHub release with every file attached, publish to PyPI with Trusted Publishing, and publish the GitHub release last. The build stays the repository's own; the three release steps are actions from here. The release-notes action needs the full history and tags (fetch-depth: 0), and the release jobs need contents: write. A complete example:

# Publishing: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
#
# Runs on the v* tags that the release workflow pushes: build, draft the GitHub release
# with every file attached, publish to PyPI, then publish the GitHub release, which makes
# it immutable. Never on `release: published`. Only the build job is repository-specific.
name: Publish

on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  # A publish run must never be cut short half-way through.
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    name: Build sdist and wheel
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.2
      - name: Build distributions
        run: uv build --out-dir dist
      - name: Check the version matches the release tag
        run: |
          expected="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          wheels=(dist/*.whl)
          actual="$(basename "${wheels[0]}" | cut -d- -f2)"
          if [[ "$actual" != "$expected" ]]; then
            echo "::error::built version is '$actual', but the release tag is '$expected'"
            exit 1
          fi
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/*

  draft_release:
    # Immutable releases: files can only be attached while the release is a draft.
    name: Create the draft GitHub release
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # git-cliff needs the full history and the tags
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      - id: notes
        uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/release-notes@v1.2.0
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/draft-release@v1.2.0
        with:
          notes-file: ${{ steps.notes.outputs.path }}
          files: |
            dist/*

  upload_pypi:
    name: Upload to PyPI
    needs: draft_release
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: pypi
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      attestations: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v4.2.2
        with:
          subject-path: "dist/*"
      - uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@v1.14.3

  publish_release:
    # Publishing locks the tag and the files and creates GitHub's release attestation.
    name: Publish the GitHub release
    needs: upload_pypi
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/publish-release@v1.2.0

release-notes writes the tag's changelog entry for a final release (git cliff --current) and everything since the last final release for a pre-release (git cliff --unreleased --tag vX.Y.0rcN), and outputs the file's path. draft-release takes notes-file and files (one glob per line, each must match), and marks alphas, betas and release candidates as pre-releases. publish-release publishes the draft. All three default to the tag that triggered the run (tag input) and to github.token (token input), and need pipx, which GitHub-hosted runners have.

items.title: justfile: preview the changelog
items.text:
just changelog shows what the next release's entry will look like, with the central cliff.toml at the version the stubs pin (read from release.yml, so Dependabot's updates carry over). If release-tools is public:

git_cliff := "git-cliff==2.14.2"

# Preview the changelog entry of the next release, with the central cliff.toml at the version release.yml pins.
changelog:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    ref=$(sed -nE 's|.*Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/release.yml@([^[:space:]]+).*|\1|p' \
        .github/workflows/release.yml)
    # Link the PR numbers like the release PR does: GitHub Actions sets GITHUB_REPOSITORY.
    repo=$(git remote get-url origin | sed -E 's#^.*github\.com[:/]##; s#\.git$##')
    GITHUB_REPOSITORY="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY:-$repo}" uvx --from {{ git_cliff }} git-cliff --unreleased \
        --config-url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools/$ref/cliff.toml"

--config-url only works for a public repository. If release-tools is internal or private, fetch the file with the GitHub CLI instead (any member who has run gh auth login):

git_cliff := "git-cliff==2.14.2"

# Preview the changelog entry of the next release, with the central cliff.toml at the version release.yml pins.
changelog:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    ref=$(sed -nE 's|.*Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/release.yml@([^[:space:]]+).*|\1|p' \
        .github/workflows/release.yml)
    # release-tools isn't public: fetch cliff.toml with the GitHub CLI (`gh auth login`).
    config="$(mktemp -d)/cliff.toml"
    gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.raw" \
        "repos/Algorithmiq/release-tools/contents/cliff.toml?ref=$ref" > "$config"
    # Link the PR numbers like the release PR does: GitHub Actions sets GITHUB_REPOSITORY.
    repo=$(git remote get-url origin | sed -E 's#^.*github\.com[:/]##; s#\.git$##')
    GITHUB_REPOSITORY="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY:-$repo}" uvx --from {{ git_cliff }} git-cliff --unreleased \
        --config "$config"

items.title: PR template
items.text:
The changelog copies the PR description's ## Migration section, up to the next ## heading, into the entry of a breaking change or deprecation. Keep the section above any later heading of the template (such as a checklist), so that only the notes are copied, and never make it the last thing in the description (see Caveats):

<!-- Keep this section above the Checklist: the changelog takes everything up to the next heading. -->
## Migration
<!-- Required for breaking changes (!) and deprecations. Delete otherwise.
     What do users need to change? Show a before/after example if possible. -->

## Checklist

- [ ] Bug fix for the current release: add the `backport` label (or ask a maintainer to)

items.title: Branching model
items.text:
release/X.Y is created at the feature freeze: the first beta, or the first release candidate when there are no betas. Alphas never create a branch. Each step below is the same history, later.

1. v1.1.0 is out. release/1.1 was cut at v1.1.0rc1; merging its release PR tagged v1.1.0, and the changelog was copied back to main. Features keep landing on main.

gitGraph TB:
  commit id: "feat: A" tag: "v1.1.0rc1"
  branch release/1.1
  commit id: "release v1.1.0" tag: "v1.1.0"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.0"
  commit id: "feat: B"

2. Alphas. Release, minor, alpha tags main's HEAD; each rerun tags the next alpha. No branch, no release PR. Features keep landing.

gitGraph TB:
  commit id: "feat: A" tag: "v1.1.0rc1"
  branch release/1.1
  commit id: "release v1.1.0" tag: "v1.1.0"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.0"
  commit id: "feat: B" tag: "v1.2.0a1"
  commit id: "feat: C" tag: "v1.2.0a2"

3. Beta: the feature freeze. Release, minor, beta cuts release/1.2 at main's HEAD and tags v1.2.0b1; the release PR opens as a draft. feat: E lands on main after the freeze, so it waits for 1.3. fix: F gets the backport label: because 1.2 is in pre-release, it goes to both lines, tagging v1.2.0b2 and updating the v1.1.1 release PR, which a maintainer merges.

gitGraph TB:
  commit id: "feat: A" tag: "v1.1.0rc1"
  branch release/1.1
  commit id: "release v1.1.0" tag: "v1.1.0"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.0"
  commit id: "feat: B" tag: "v1.2.0a1"
  commit id: "feat: C" tag: "v1.2.0a2"
  commit id: "feat: D" tag: "v1.2.0b1"
  branch release/1.2
  checkout main
  commit id: "feat: E"
  commit id: "fix: F"
  checkout release/1.2
  cherry-pick id: "fix: F" tag: "v1.2.0b2"
  checkout release/1.1
  cherry-pick id: "fix: F" tag: ""
  commit id: "release v1.1.1" tag: "v1.1.1"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.1"

4. Release candidates. Release, minor, rc promotes 1.2: it tags v1.2.0rc1 on the branch HEAD (the same commit as v1.2.0b2) and marks the release PR ready. The next backport, fix: G, tags v1.2.0rc2 and still reaches 1.1 (pending v1.1.2).

gitGraph TB:
  commit id: "feat: A" tag: "v1.1.0rc1"
  branch release/1.1
  commit id: "release v1.1.0" tag: "v1.1.0"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.0"
  commit id: "feat: B" tag: "v1.2.0a1"
  commit id: "feat: C" tag: "v1.2.0a2"
  commit id: "feat: D" tag: "v1.2.0b1"
  branch release/1.2
  checkout main
  commit id: "feat: E"
  commit id: "fix: F"
  checkout release/1.2
  cherry-pick id: "fix: F" tag: "v1.2.0b2 + v1.2.0rc1"
  checkout release/1.1
  cherry-pick id: "fix: F" tag: ""
  commit id: "release v1.1.1" tag: "v1.1.1"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.1"
  commit id: "fix: G"
  checkout release/1.2
  cherry-pick id: "fix: G" tag: "v1.2.0rc2"
  checkout release/1.1
  cherry-pick id: "fix: G" tag: ""

5. Final and patches. The pending v1.1.2 is merged, then the 1.2 release PR, which tags v1.2.0. From now on 1.1 is unsupported and backports go to release/1.2 only: fix: H updates the v1.2.1 release PR, and merging it ships the patch, with no pre-releases.

gitGraph TB:
  commit id: "feat: A" tag: "v1.1.0rc1"
  branch release/1.1
  commit id: "release v1.1.0" tag: "v1.1.0"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.0"
  commit id: "feat: B" tag: "v1.2.0a1"
  commit id: "feat: C" tag: "v1.2.0a2"
  commit id: "feat: D" tag: "v1.2.0b1"
  branch release/1.2
  checkout main
  commit id: "feat: E"
  commit id: "fix: F"
  checkout release/1.2
  cherry-pick id: "fix: F" tag: "v1.2.0b2 + v1.2.0rc1"
  checkout release/1.1
  cherry-pick id: "fix: F" tag: ""
  commit id: "release v1.1.1" tag: "v1.1.1"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.1"
  commit id: "fix: G"
  checkout release/1.2
  cherry-pick id: "fix: G" tag: "v1.2.0rc2"
  checkout release/1.1
  cherry-pick id: "fix: G" tag: ""
  commit id: "release v1.1.2" tag: "v1.1.2"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.2"
  checkout release/1.2
  commit id: "release v1.2.0" tag: "v1.2.0"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.2.0"
  commit id: "fix: H"
  checkout release/1.2
  cherry-pick id: "fix: H" tag: ""
  commit id: "release v1.2.1" tag: "v1.2.1"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.2.1"

The diagrams leave out the bot's release-pr/X.Y, changelog/vX.Y.Z and backport branches, and the commits that record the version for pre-release tags when a repository has version files.

items.title: Caveats
items.text:
• Trailers. git-cliff reads Key: value lines at the end of a commit message as git trailers and drops them from the body. A PR description that ends with its Migration section, or whose notes end with Before: … / After: … lines, loses those lines from the changelog. Keep the Migration section above a later heading of the template, and write before/after examples as code blocks. (tests/test_cliff.py pins this behaviour.)
  • The changelog PR merges itself, without a review or its checks. After a final release the bot opens a PR adding the release's section of CHANGELOG.md to main and merges it at once with its bypass of the main ruleset (gh pr merge --admin): the section was already reviewed in the release PR, and CI runs on main after the merge. Without the bypass (Per-repository setup, step 8) the job enables auto-merge instead, with a warning, and the PR waits for an approval: auto-merge never bypasses a ruleset. If a changelog PR conflicts (two finals released close together), re-run its "Release" workflow run's sync job: it checks out main, rebuilds changelog/vX.Y.Z from the current main with git checkout -B, and force-pushes it.
  • Check names. The PR checks report as PR checks / PR title and PR checks / Migration notes. A repository that required the contexts PR title and Migration notes of its own copy must switch its rulesets to the new names right after merging the stub: pull_request_target runs the workflow file of main, so the PR adding the stub still reports the old names, and every later PR the new ones.
  • job.workflow_* is GitHub.com-only (not on GitHub Enterprise Server), and actionlint 1.7.12 doesn't know it yet: .github/actionlint.yaml ignores the two properties in release.yml and backport.yml. Consumers' stubs don't use it.
  • The release and backport jobs check release-tools out into .release-tools/ inside the caller's working tree. It is never added to a commit: the workflow only adds CHANGELOG.md and the version files, and excludes .release-tools/ via .git/info/exclude.
  • An older release line runs its own version of the workflows. Each push to release/X.Y runs the workflow files of that branch, whose stub pins the release-tools version of the time the branch was created. A patch release of an older line therefore runs that older release-tools (for release-tools itself: its own older workflows), with that version's behaviour and texts. Bump the pin on an older line only if its patch releases need a fix of release-tools.
  • Changelog entries of backports link the backport PR. The changelog lists the PR that was squash-merged into each branch: a fix backported to two lines appears as, say, #15 under one and #16 under the other, not as the original PR on main. Each backport PR's description links the original ("Backport of #14").
  • Concurrency. The release jobs queue per ref in the group release-<ref> of the calling repository. A promotion runs in main's group, so a backport merged into release/X.Y at the same moment may briefly leave the release PR or a beta tag out of step; the next push to the branch puts the PR right.

items.title: What is central and what stays per repository
items.text:
Piece Where Per-repository input Release logic: start a release, alphas, betas and release candidates, the release PR, final tag, the changelog on main .github/workflows/release.yml (reusable) version-files Versions, tags, the release PR, the changelog on main release/: versions, tagging, changelog, workflow, release_pr (standard library only), run by release.yml and backport.yml none Changelog format cliff.toml, used by release.yml, the release-notes action and the local preview none Backport PRs for the backport label, and the suggestion on fixes merged without it .github/workflows/backport.yml (reusable) none PR title and migration notes checks .github/workflows/pr-checks.yml (reusable) none Release notes for a tag actions/release-notes (composite) none Draft GitHub release with files actions/draft-release (composite) the files to attach Publish the draft release actions/publish-release (composite) none Triggers, permissions, the bot's credentials each repository's stubs Build, version check, PyPI upload each repository's publish workflow (deploy.yml) everything just changelog each repository's justfile none PR template with the Migration section each repository's .github/pull_request_template.md anything else in it CHANGELOG.md each repository, written by the bot

PR titles use the types feat fix deprecate perf docs refactor test build ci chore style in every repository. The first five appear in the changelog; the others are left out unless they are breaking (!). A gitmoji after the type (feat: ✨ add X, or :sparkles:) is optional and stripped from the changelog. The changelog starts at the newest final tag, so a repository tags v0.0.0 where it adopts the process. Each entry ends with an absolute link to its PR ([#12](https://github.com/…/pull/12)), built from GITHUB_REPOSITORY: GitHub doesn't autolink #12 in CHANGELOG.md, nor reliably in release notes. The just changelog recipes take the repository from the origin remote.
path: What is central and what stays per repository

items.title: How the central files reach the caller at the pinned version
items.text:
Inside a reusable workflow the github context is the caller's (docs), so github.sha and github.workflow_ref say nothing about release-tools. Three options were considered:

  • (a) job.workflow_repository and job.workflow_sha, chosen. The job context identifies the workflow file that defines the current job; for a reusable workflow, the called file. GitHub documents exactly this use: a reusable workflow checking out its own repository at job.workflow_sha (job context; added to the docs in github/docs#60709, April 2026; used in production by github/gh-aw). release.yml checks out ${{ job.workflow_repository }} at ${{ job.workflow_sha }}, the commit of the tag the caller pinned, so the workflow logic, the release package and cliff.toml always come from one ref. It costs the stubs nothing.
  • (b) Composite actions called from the reusable workflow. A composite action sees its files through github.action_path, but a reusable workflow calling Algorithmiq/release-tools/<action>@<ref> must hard-code <ref>. The workflow at v1.2.0 would then run actions from whatever tag was written into it, unless every release rewrote its own references before tagging, which the release process can't do (the tag doesn't exist yet when the release PR is written). Rejected.
  • © Consumers calling composite actions directly. Version-consistent, but each stub would carry the jobs, conditions, token steps and checkouts that make up most of release.yml: about a hundred lines per repository instead of thirty. Rejected.

The checkout of release-tools uses a second token of the release bot, limited to contents: read on release-tools (repositories and permission-* inputs). For a public release-tools that token isn't needed, but it keeps one code path for every visibility: an internal or private repository can't be read with the caller's GITHUB_TOKEN, and the Actions Access setting only lets the runner download actions and reusable workflows, not check the repository out (docs).

backport.yml checks release-tools out the same way, for its backport-targets command; pr-checks.yml needs no files from here. The publish actions are composite actions called directly from the consumer's deploy.yml, where the consumer writes the ref: release-notes finds cliff.toml at ${{ github.action_path }}/../../cliff.toml, which the runner downloads with the action at that ref.

items.title: Secrets and inputs
items.text: The stubs pass client-id and private-key explicitly. secrets: inherit would also work, but would hand every secret of the repository to release-tools and hide which one it needs. Workflow-level env of the caller does not reach a reusable workflow (docs), hence the version-files input.

items.title: Enforcing the PR checks with an organisation ruleset
items.text:
An organisation ruleset can require workflows to pass before merging, running a workflow from release-tools in every targeted repository with no stub at all (docs). It is an option, not the default, because of these caveats:

  • It needs GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
  • Ruleset workflows only run for the default activity types: opened, synchronize and reopened for pull_request_target; types filters are ignored (docs). Editing a PR's title or description does not re-run the checks, which defeats a title check: a fixed title stays red until the next push.
  • The enforced file must trigger on pull_request or pull_request_target, so it would be a wrapper such as self-pr-checks.yml rather than the reusable pr-checks.yml. Whether its ./.github/workflows/pr-checks.yml reference resolves to release-tools when run as a ruleset workflow in another repository is unverified.
  • The workflow's repository must be at least as visible as the targeted ones (a public one works everywhere), with the Access setting if it isn't public.
  • The rule blocks direct pushes on the targeted branches. Rulesets for release/* must use "Do not require workflow checks on creation" so that the bot can still create the branches. PRs opened before the rule only get the checks after their next push.

The upside is central enforcement that a repository can't remove. Reconsider it if the edited limitation is lifted.

items.title: Developing release-tools
items.text:
just build    # uv sync: pytest, ruff, ty, prek, git-cliff, shellcheck
just lint     # every hook: ruff, ty, actionlint (+ shellcheck), workflow and action schemas
just test     # the release package, cliff.toml, the actions, and that the examples match
  • tests/test_release.py covers each command of the release package (tests/test_cli.py its entry points and help); tests/test_release_e2e.py drives whole release flows (two series; alphas, betas, candidates and two release lines with the changelog on main) the way release.yml and backport.yml do, against a scratch repository with a local bare origin and a stand-in for gh; tests/test_release_pr.py runs its release-pr command; tests/test_workflows.py checks that the workflows only read outputs the package writes.
  • tests/test_cliff.py runs git-cliff 2.14.2 on scratch histories: gitmoji stripping, migration notes, blank lines, ignored pre-releases, two release lines, --current, --prepend.
  • tests/test_actions.py shellchecks the composite actions and runs them with stand-ins for pipx and gh.
  • tests/test_examples.py checks that docs/adopting.md, the examples/ and the dogfooding stubs agree, that the stubs pass what the reusable workflows declare, and that every reference uses the same release-tools tag and git-cliff version.

Requires Python 3.12 or later: the release package runs on the runner's system Python (python3 path/to/release <command>) and only uses the standard library. python3 release --help lists its commands.

items.title: How release-tools releases itself
items.text:
release-tools follows the same process with its own workflows (dogfooding): self-release.yml, self-backport.yml and self-pr-checks.yml are the consumer stubs with uses: ./.github/workflows/<file> instead of a pinned tag, and self-publish.yml publishes the GitHub release with ./actions/*. A local reference runs the workflow from the same commit as the event, so a change is exercised by release-tools itself (release candidates included) before any consumer pins it. Nothing is built or uploaded: the release is the tag and its notes.

It has no version files (version-files: ""). Set it up like any other repository (Per-repository setup, without PyPI), tag v0.0.0 on the first commit, and start the first release with major to get v1.0.0rc1 and then v1.0.0.

items.title: The documentation site
items.text:
The pages in docs/ are the source of https://algorithmiq.github.io/release-tools/, built with Zensical (zensical.toml). just docs previews it with live reload; just docs-build builds it the way CI does (--strict: broken links fail). Links between pages are relative .md links, so they work on GitHub too.

Each release deploys its version with Zensical's fork of mike (the docs job of .github/workflows/self-publish.yml), which commits to the gh-pages branch:

Tag Deployed as vX.Y.Z, newest final line X.Y, and latest moves to it vX.Y.Z, an older line X.Y (latest stays) vX.Y.0aN, bN, rcN X.Y, titled "X.Y (pre-release)", until its final replaces it

The site root redirects to latest after the first final; until then, it redirects to the first pre-release's line. If a docs deploy is skipped because several tags were pushed close together, re-run that tag's docs job (the deploy logic doesn't depend on order, so it's safe in any order). mike is transitional: when Zensical ships native versioning, only the deploy step changes.

One-time setup, by a repository admin: Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). The branch appears with the first deploy; set the source after it. No ruleset may block pushes of the Actions token to gh-pages.

items.title: Open questions
items.text:
• Visibility of release-tools (public preferred). Everything works either way; see One-time organisation setup for what an internal or private repository needs.
  • Dependabot and pre-releases. Whether Dependabot proposes vX.Y.0aN, bN or rcN tags of release-tools as updates is untested: it shows only in a repository that pins release-tools while one of its pre-releases is out. If it does, add an ignore rule for them.

items.title: Answered by the v1.2.0 release
items.text:
release-tools released v1.2.0 through two betas, a release candidate and the final, with v1.1.1 shipped from the previous line in between. That answered:

  • Auto-merge of the changelog PR doesn't bypass review: the PR waited for an approval. The bot now merges it with its ruleset bypass instead; see Caveats.
  • job.workflow_* on real runs resolve to release-tools at the pinned commit, so the jobs run the release package and cliff.toml of the same version as the workflows.
  • Pages builds after mike deploy --push with GITHUB_TOKEN: the push triggers "pages build and deployment". The very first build, right after Pages is enabled, takes a few minutes, and the site returns 404 until it finishes.
  • The backport suggestion comment works with the bot's Pull requests: write permission; no Issues permission is needed.

items.title: One-time organisation setup
items.text:
An organisation owner does this once. The commands need gh with the admin:org scope (gh auth refresh -h github.com -s admin:org) and jq.

  1. Create the release bot GitHub App (web UI only): https://github.com/organizations/Algorithmiq/settings/apps/new.
  2. Name algorithmiq-release-bot; homepage https://github.com/Algorithmiq; webhook not active.
  3. Repository permissions: Contents read and write (release branches, tags, the changelog), Pull requests read and write (release, backport and changelog PRs, merging the changelog PRs, the backport suggestions), Workflows read and write (pushing branches whose commits touch .github/workflows/). Metadata read-only is added automatically. Nothing else, no events. Installable only on this account.
  4. Note the App ID (a number, for the rulesets) and the Client ID (Iv23…, for the workflows). Generate a private key and keep the .pem only until step 2.
  5. Install it on release-tools and on every repository that adopts the process. release-tools needs it for its own releases, and the release workflow uses it to read release-tools when that repository is not public.
  6. Store the credentials for the repositories that use them, release-tools included (--repos replaces the list, so always pass all of them):
gh variable set RELEASE_BOT_CLIENT_ID --org Algorithmiq --visibility selected \
  --repos release-tools,AEGISS --body "$CLIENT_ID"
gh secret set RELEASE_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY --org Algorithmiq --visibility selected \
  --repos release-tools,AEGISS < algorithmiq-release-bot.*.private-key.pem
  1. Allow the actions. If the organisation restricts which actions and reusable workflows may run, allow Algorithmiq/release-tools/* and the actions it uses (actions/checkout, actions/create-github-app-token, amannn/action-semantic-pull-request, korthout/backport-action). The allow list of the calling repository applies to everything a reusable workflow uses.
  2. Visibility of release-tools. Public is simplest and preferred. If it is internal or private instead:
  3. release-tools → Settings → Actions → General → Access: "Accessible from repositories in the 'Algorithmiq' organization". Without it, no other repository can call its workflows or actions. (docs)
  4. A public repository can only call public workflows, so release-tools must be public as soon as any public repository adopts it. (docs)
  5. "Internal" exists only with GitHub Enterprise Cloud; otherwise it is private.
  6. Dependabot needs access to release-tools to update the pins: add it to the organisation's "Grant Dependabot access to private repositories" list (in the organisation's code security settings).
  7. Local changelog previews use the gh variant of just changelog.

Nothing in the workflows changes: they read release-tools with a read-only token of the release bot either way (see Design).

items.title: Patch releases
items.text:
Patch releases are not started from the Release workflow: they come from the backport label.

  1. Fix the bug on main as usual, with a fix: (or perf:) PR.
  2. Add the backport label to the PR, before or after merging it. If it is merged without the label, the bot comments on it with the versions the label would ship it in.
  3. The bot cherry-picks the fix onto release/X.Y and opens a backport PR with the same title. If the cherry-pick conflicts, the PR is a draft with the conflict committed: resolve it on that branch and mark it ready. Merging the first backport opens the release PR chore: release vX.Y.Z; later ones are added to it.
  4. Merge the release PR when the fixes should ship. The bot tags vX.Y.Z, which is published like any release, with no alphas, betas or release candidates.

For example, with v1.1.0 out, fix: crash on empty input is merged into main, and a maintainer adds the backport label a day later. The bot opens the backport PR into release/1.1; merging it opens chore: release v1.1.1; merging that releases v1.1.1. While 1.2 is in beta or release candidates, the same label also opens a backport PR into release/1.2, which tags its next beta or candidate.

items.title: The release process
items.text: Every repository that adopts release-tools works this way. People only make decisions: start a release, move it to its next stage, label fixes for backporting, and approve the changelog. The release bot does the rest.

items.title: Branches
items.text:
Branch Purpose Lifetime main Where all work lands, through squash-merged pull requests. Always releasable. Alphas are tagged here. Permanent release/X.Y Created at the feature freeze of release X.Y: its betas, release candidates, X.Y.0 and patch releases. Only receives bug fixes backported from main. Until the next minor or major release is final; then it is unsupported release-pr/X.Y, changelog/vX.Y.Z, backport branches The bot's branches for its PRs Managed by the bot Work branches (e.g. fix/login-timeout) One change, one pull request Deleted after merging

Patches go to the newest final release. While the next release is in beta or release candidates, fixes are backported to both; older releases get no fixes, and users upgrade.

items.title: Pull requests
items.text:
• Branch off main and target main, bug fixes included. Only the bot opens PRs against release branches.
  • PRs are squash-merged, so the PR title and description become the commit. The title becomes the changelog entry, so write it for users: type: description, with an optional scope (fix(io): …), an optional gitmoji after the colon (fix(io): 🐛 …, stripped from the changelog), and ! after the type for a breaking change (feat!: remove the old solver API).
Type Use for In the changelog feat new functionality Features fix bug fixes Fixes deprecate marking something as deprecated Deprecations, with the migration notes perf performance improvements Performance docs documentation only Documentation refactor, test, build, ci, chore, style changes users don't notice no (unless breaking)
  • Breaking changes and deprecations need a ## Migration section in the PR description saying what users have to change, with a before/after example as code blocks. It is copied into the changelog under the entry, which lists breaking changes first.
  • The PR checks enforce the title format and the Migration section, and re-run when the title or description is edited.
  • A bug fix that should also reach the current release gets the backport label, before or after merging: see Patch releases. Features are never backported.

items.title: Versions
items.text:
Semantic versioning, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Patch releases only fix bugs and never break anything. Before 1.0, a minor release may break existing code; from 1.0 on, only a major release may. Tags carry a v prefix (v0.5.0, v0.5.0rc1).

A release started from the Release workflow (X.Y.0, including 0.Y.0 and 1.0.0) can have pre-releases, spelled as in PEP 440:

Stage Tag On Pre-1.0 1.0 and later Alpha: features still landing (optional) vX.Y.0aN main v0.5.0a1 v1.3.0a1, v2.0.0a1 Beta: feature freeze, fixes only (optional) vX.Y.0bN release/X.Y v0.5.0b1 v1.3.0b1 Release candidate (at least one) vX.Y.0rcN release/X.Y v0.5.0rc1 v1.3.0rc1 Final vX.Y.0 release/X.Y v0.5.0 v1.3.0 Patch vX.Y.Z release/X.Y v0.5.1 v1.3.1

Patch releases (X.Y.Z with Z > 0) never have alphas, betas or release candidates, before or after 1.0: merging their release PR ships them directly.

Public functionality is deprecated before it is removed: it keeps working and emits a DeprecationWarning naming the replacement and the earliest version that removes it, for at least one minor release (from 1.0 on, until the next major release). The removal is then a breaking change with migration notes. Names starting with _ and anything documented as experimental are exempt.

items.title: Releasing
items.text:
Steps 1–3 are runs of Actions → Release → Run workflow on main, with a bump (minor or major, counted from the newest final release) and a stage. Before starting, a maintainer checks that no deprecation is due for removal.

  1. Alphas (optional). Stage alpha tags vX.Y.0aN on main, published as a pre-release. Run it again for the next alpha; features keep landing on main.
  2. Betas (optional): the feature freeze. Stage beta creates release/X.Y from main, tags vX.Y.0b1 and opens the release PR chore: release vX.Y.0 as a draft. From then on only backported fixes reach X.Y: each one merged into release/X.Y tags the next beta and updates the release PR. Features merged into main wait for the next release.
  3. Release candidates. Stage rc promotes a release in beta: it tags vX.Y.0rc1 on release/X.Y and marks the release PR ready for review. Without betas, it creates release/X.Y with vX.Y.0rc1 and opens the release PR. Every backport then tags the next candidate. Testing pre-releases is optional (pip install --pre <package>==X.Y.0rcN).
  4. Release. A maintainer reviews the changelog in the release PR and merges it. The bot tags vX.Y.0; the repository's publish workflow builds, drafts the GitHub release with every file attached, publishes to PyPI and publishes the release, which makes it immutable. The bot then adds the release's section of CHANGELOG.md to main through a PR that it merges itself, and closes the pending patch release PR of the previous line, if any: its support ends here, and its fixes are in X.Y.0. Merge that PR first to ship them.

The workflow refuses to go backwards (an alpha once release/X.Y exists, a beta once it is at release candidates), and to create a release branch while another one has no final release yet. CHANGELOG.md on main lists every final release of every line; to reword an older section, edit it on main with a normal PR (a release PR only adds its own section to main).

A published release never changes. A broken one is yanked on PyPI and replaced by a new patch release. Only the bot creates v* tags.

items.title: Per-repository setup
items.text:
A repository admin does this when a repository adopts the process. Set REPO=Algorithmiq/<name> and APP_ID=<the App ID> first. Steps 1 to 7 come before merging the PR that adds the stubs, 8 after it.

  1. Install the app and share the credentials with the repository: add it to the app's installation (Organisation settings → GitHub Apps → algorithmiq-release-bot → Configure), and to the --repos lists of the variable and the secret.
  2. Tag v0.0.0, the start of the changelog, on the last commit that should not appear in it, before the tag ruleset (step 5) exists. The first release is then 0.1.0 (or 1.0.0 when started with major).
git tag -a v0.0.0 -m "Start of the changelog" <commit>
git push origin v0.0.0
just changelog    # what the first release will contain
  1. Settings. Squash-merge only, with the PR title and description as the commit message (otherwise the migration notes never reach the changelog), auto-merge, automatic deletion of head branches, immutable releases, and the backport label:
gh api -X PATCH repos/$REPO -F allow_squash_merge=true -F allow_merge_commit=false \
  -F allow_rebase_merge=false -F allow_auto_merge=true -F delete_branch_on_merge=true \
  -f squash_merge_commit_title=PR_TITLE -f squash_merge_commit_message=PR_BODY
gh api -X PUT repos/$REPO/immutable-releases
gh label create backport -R $REPO --color B60205 \
  --description "Also ship this fix in the current release"
  1. Files. The three stubs, the publish workflow, the justfile recipe, the Migration section of the PR template, an empty CHANGELOG.md if there is none, and the Dependabot group. Delete any local copies of release.py and cliff.toml.
  2. Tag ruleset: only the release bot creates, moves or deletes v* tags.
gh api -X POST repos/$REPO/rulesets --input - <<EOF
{"name": "release tags", "target": "tag", "enforcement": "active",
 "conditions": {"ref_name": {"include": ["refs/tags/v*"], "exclude": []}},
 "rules": [{"type": "creation"}, {"type": "update"}, {"type": "deletion"}],
 "bypass_actors": [{"actor_id": $APP_ID, "actor_type": "Integration", "bypass_mode": "always"}]}
EOF
  1. release/* ruleset: changes only through squash-merged PRs that pass CI, and only the bot creates the branches. List the repository's own required checks next to the PR checks (15368 is the GitHub Actions app, which reports them):
gh api -X POST repos/$REPO/rulesets --input - <<EOF
{"name": "release branches", "target": "branch", "enforcement": "active",
 "conditions": {"ref_name": {"include": ["refs/heads/release/*"], "exclude": []}},
 "rules": [
  {"type": "creation"}, {"type": "deletion"}, {"type": "non_fast_forward"}, {"type": "required_linear_history"},
  {"type": "pull_request", "parameters": {"allowed_merge_methods": ["squash"], "dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push": true,
    "require_code_owner_review": false, "require_last_push_approval": false,
    "required_approving_review_count": 1, "required_review_thread_resolution": false}},
  {"type": "required_status_checks", "parameters": {"strict_required_status_checks_policy": true,
    "required_status_checks": [{"context": "PR checks / PR title", "integration_id": 15368},
      {"context": "PR checks / Migration notes", "integration_id": 15368}]}}],
 "bypass_actors": [{"actor_id": $APP_ID, "actor_type": "Integration", "bypass_mode": "always"}]}
EOF
  1. PyPI Trusted Publishing for the publish workflow: on PyPI, add a (pending) publisher with the repository, the workflow file name and the environment (pypi in the example). The first pre-release is published to PyPI straight away.
  2. After the stubs are on main: require the PR checks on main and let the bot bypass the main ruleset. pull_request_target runs the workflow file of the base branch, so the checks never report until the stub is on main; requiring them earlier blocks every PR, including the one adding them. The bypass lets the bot merge its changelog PR at once, without a review or the PR checks (see Caveats); without it, each changelog PR waits for a maintainer's approval.
id=$(gh api repos/$REPO/rulesets --jq '.[] | select(.name == "main") | .id')
gh api repos/$REPO/rulesets/$id | jq --argjson app "$APP_ID" '{name, target, enforcement, conditions,
  rules: (.rules | map(if .type == "required_status_checks"
    then .parameters.required_status_checks += [{"context": "PR checks / PR title", "integration_id": 15368},
                                                {"context": "PR checks / Migration notes", "integration_id": 15368}]
    else . end)),
  bypass_actors: (.bypass_actors + [{"actor_id": $app, "actor_type": "Integration", "bypass_mode": "always"}])}' \
| gh api -X PUT repos/$REPO/rulesets/$id --input -

This assumes a main ruleset with a required_status_checks rule; create one first if there is none.

The first release: check that no deprecation is due for removal, then Actions → Release → Run workflow on main (or gh workflow run release.yml -R $REPO --ref main -f bump=minor -f stage=rc).

items.title: Versioning and upgrading
items.text:
release-tools follows the release process itself and uses Semantic Versioning from 1.0.0:

  • Major: consumers must change something: a stub's inputs, secrets or required permissions, the names of the PR checks, or the release behaviour.
  • Minor: new optional inputs or features, changelog format changes that need no action.
  • Patch: fixes.

Consumers pin an exact tag (@v1.2.0) in all three stubs and in the actions of the publish workflow, and keep them in step. Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem updates both reusable workflows and actions; group them so that one PR moves every reference:

version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    groups:
      release-tools:
        patterns:
          - "Algorithmiq/release-tools*"

Pre-releases of release-tools (v1.2.0b1, v1.2.0rc1) are real tags: pin one in a repository to try a change before it is released. Immutable releases make every published tag permanent, so a pinned version can never change under a consumer.

items.title: Upgrading to v1.2.0
items.text:
v1.2.0 brings alphas and betas, and changes visible to existing consumers:

  • Dual backports during every release candidate window. With the default stage: rc, every release now has an rc window during which backports go to both lines: the branch in pre-release and the newest released branch. The previous line gets a backport PR and a patch release PR, which the X.Y.0 final closes.
  • Backport suggestion comment. Merged fix and perf PRs without the backport label get a comment suggesting it.
  • sync-changelog adds only the release's own section to main. Wording fixes a release PR makes to older sections no longer reach main.
  • The stub needs the stage input. Pin v1.2.0 and add stage: to the stub's inputs, with the same description, type, required and default as in release.yml.
